Hi all — following vaguely on from the discussion in this thread, I have sketched out what it might look like to formalise "this SKI term computes this function" in a more systematic way. You can see how it looks on my fork, but more-or-less the idea is that a type α is Encoded if it is equipped with a predicate IsEncoding : α → SKI → Prop, which we already have for eg Nat, Bool, Nat \x Nat, etc. Then we can extend this to functions by a logical relation: xf encodes f: α → β if xf ⬝ xa encodes f a for any xa encoding a.

To stress-test it I have encoded a the types and constructions we have so far (in a suitably generalised way) — for instance I've cooked up a term which encodes List.rec : β → (α → List α → β → β) → List α → β, for any encoded types α, β.

I'll put it up in a PR soon, but I wanted to call for any comments here first since it will probably require moving some imports around & might be a moderately intimidating diff — particularly from @Jesse Alama who has been working on this corner of the library

A couple of notes:

  • The requirement that the encoding be faithful (ie equivalent terms do not represent distinct elements) is very reasonable and probably necessary for the encoding to be meaningful, but technically it seems separate. As such I might move that discussion to Evaluation.lean (or something depending on it) which is where the injectivity results are currently proven.
  • We require in the class Encoded that "y encodes a and x reduces to y implies x encodes a", which is the fact we've been using in the existing examples. I think this is right: it says that the what you encode only depends on the outcome of any computation.
  • We don't require the opposite, that encoding descends to reducts of a term. I think this is true for Nat and Bool at least, but seems delicate to prove — I'm unsure whether it will extend to higher types.

At first glance that module looks reasonable to me, but it seems useful to generalize? For example starting with

class Encoded (α : Type _) {β} (r : β → β → Prop) where
  IsEncoding : α → β → Prop
  isEncoding_of_red {a : α} {b₁ b₂ : β} : IsEncoding a b₂ → r b₁ b₂ → IsEncoding a b₁

and similarly for the classes that extend it.

Brilliant! We're doing some work on encodings and their correctness at FORM, so it'd be useful to find a common interface, as @Chris Henson commented.

We're working with LTS though, so I don't expect much interplay yet outside of the basic definition of encoding. The only thing I can notice is that I have a class for Encodings that simply gives access to the usual notation for them:

class Encoding (α β : Type*) where
  /-- The encoding from `α` to `β`. -/
  encoding (α : a) : β

@[inherit_doc]
scoped notation:29 "⟦" a "⟧" => Encoding.encoding a

You can safely ignore this for now, I just wanted to give you a heads up. Just make sure you namespace everything so that we don't have a conflict, as your definitions seem pretty specialised to either SKI or reduction systems (and even there mapping of reductions is a strong requirement that often doesn't hold for complex encodings).

Great, this all sounds good! I didn't define a general class because I suspected the definitions might be quite specific (for reasons along the lines that Fabrizio mentions) — perhaps something like this could be fairly innocuous:

/-- Types encoded some calculus. -/
class Encoded (α β : Type _) where
  /-- An element is represented by a term. -/
  IsEncoding : α → β → Prop

def IsEncoding [Encoded α β] : α → β → Prop := Encoded.IsEncoding

-- scoped
notation x " ⊩ " a => IsEncoding a x

/-- Types for which encodings are invariant by anti-reduction. -/
class EncodedLift (α : Type _) {β : Type _} (r : β → β → Prop) extends Encoded α β where
  /-- Representation lifts along reductions. -/
  isEncoding_left_of_red : {a : α} → {x y : β} → (y ⊩ a) → r x y → x ⊩ a

/-- Types for which encodings are invariant by reduction. -/
class EncodedDesc (α : Type _) {β : Type _} (r : β → β → Prop) extends Encoded α β where
  /-- Representation descends along reductions. -/
  isEncoding_right_of_red : {a : α} → {x y : β} → (x ⊩ a) → r x y → y ⊩ a

/-- The encoding is faithful if no equivalent terms represent two distinct elements. -/
class FaithfullyEncoded (α : Type*) {β : Type*} (r : β → β → Prop) extends
    Encoded α β where
  eq_of_isEncoding_of_eqvGen : {a b : α} → {x y : β} → (hax : x ⊩ a) →
      (hby : y ⊩ b) → (h : Relation.EqvGen r x y) → a = b

/-- The encoding is fully if every element has an encoding. -/
class FullyEncoded (α β : Type*) extends Encoded α where
  exists_isEncoding : ∀ a : α, ∃ x : β, x ⊩ a

Does that seems suitable? Where might that definition go (& be scoped)?

There could also be a parallel class to FaithfullyEncoded for types having a "canonical encoding", which would look more like Fabrizio's version above, with a computable interpretation function α -> β, plus a certificate that the encoding satisfies our predicate ⟦a⟧ ⊩ a

What an interesting coincidence: I finally managed to wrap up a proof of equivalence of SKI and partial recursive functions. I didn't pay too much attention to encoding as such, because I just leaned on Mathlib's existing Code infrastructure. Happy to tweak things to use a Computes or Encoded typeclass if those land first.

Oh wow very cool! happy to work this out in either order depending on how long your work will take to merge — in my new formulation the statement should look something like Partrec f ↔ (∃ x : SKI, x ⊩ f) up to the definition of encodings of partial functions

Yeah I think there is a small difference running around about how the data of the reduction is carried around, but otherwise I think we're all mostly on the same page. @Thomas Waring maybe these should go in a new module under Foundations/Semantics?

Chris Henson said:

... maybe these should go in a new module under Foundations/Semantics?

sounds good — would you prefer that as a separate PR, or should I fold it in with defining those notions for SKI
Normally I'd say split it up, but it is nice to see the first use of a new definition. As long as it stays around the current size of a +550 diff, I am fine reviewing them together.
okay great — i think i’ll leave the full & faithful bits for the future which will make it a bit more reasonable too

Just commenting on the general classes:

  1. I'm a bit confused by the fact that Encoded/IsEncoded is reversed, usually the source is on the left and the mapping on the right. What's the reason for that? (For a name for the normal ordering, I'd call it 'Encodes' or something like that.) The notation then reverses it.
  2. Just double checking: you're defining the encoding as a relation rather than a function so that you can just define encodings as an inductive or similar, right? It might be a good thing for me to generalise Encoding like that as well... at that point, do we really have a difference between your Encoded and my Encoding? Could we hope to merge them?
  3. What are the uses of EncodedLift and EncodedDesc?

My current use case for Encoding is defining correctness results of encodings and full abstraction, and that's gonna be interesting both for LTS and reduction semantics, so it might make sense to converge on a shared class early on, if it makes sense. :)

Thanks for your comments!

  1. Yep I think you're right on that
  2. Not exactly, I think actually my name might be a little misleading — the idea is probably closer to "computes" (as Jesse had for partrec functions) or even "realises", it's a relation since we want to say eg SKI.Add ⬝ SKI.One ⬝ SKI.One "computes" 2, but so does SKI.Succ ⬝ SKI.One etc.
  3. This is maybe clearer with the above interpretation — since SKI.Pred ⬝ SKI.One ↠ SKI.Zero and SKI.Zero certainly computes 0, we want to say the same of SKI.Pred ⬝ SKI.One: we used this (the lift version) for all the SKI encodings we have so far. The desc one was just for symmetry.

The one part where something like your class might be useful (and actually deserve the name "encode") is if we want certain functions / data to have "canonical realisers" — eg church numerals etc

I think I'll land on Realizes (in the order Fabrizio suggests) unless there are any objections? It my definitions have the same logical-relation style extension to function types as in realisability and the lift / desc classes come up often there too

I was away from this for a while, but I've put (a tidier version of) my work up as a draft PR cslib#448. I'll wait until @Jesse Alama 's work is merged so I can express it in my notation.

I'm conscious that the diff is quite large & will only get larger with Jesse's work — currently it's +700ish lines but most of that is a mechanical rephrasing of earlier results (viz -500 lines). If anyone can see a pleasant way to split it up I am open to suggestions!
